title: Eschatology
summary: These passages describe hope for God’s future without giving one shared timetable. Daniel 7 pictures a human-like figure receiving authority; Daniel 12 speaks of awakening from the dust, including resurrection to life or shame. Matthew 24 uses cosmic signs and speaks of the Son of Man gathering the elect. First Thessalonians 4 comforts mourners with the promise that the dead in Christ will rise; First Corinthians 15 describes resurrection and the defeat of death; Revelation 21 pictures renewed creation where God dwells with humanity. Read together, the texts connect judgment, resurrection, and restoration, but each addresses a different question and uses a different image.
historical_context: The references come from apocalyptic visions, Jesus’ teaching, pastoral counsel, and a letter’s argument. Daniel 7 and 12 portray authority, crisis, and resurrection through symbolic vision. Matthew 24 answers questions about the temple’s fate and the coming of the Son of Man. First Thessalonians 4 responds to grief about believers who have died, while First Corinthians 15 argues for resurrection and the defeat of death. Revelation 21 presents a vision of renewed creation. These passages address hope and expectation; they do not provide a date or a single detailed sequence of end-time events.
canonical_context: Daniel 7 and 12 place the themes of divine rule and resurrection in visions of crisis and hope. Matthew 24 uses related Son of Man imagery in a discourse about the temple and the gathering of the elect. Paul’s letters address different pastoral questions: First Thessalonians 4 offers comfort about the dead, while First Corinthians 15 explains resurrection and the defeat of death. Revelation 21 turns the theme toward renewed creation and God’s dwelling with humanity. The sequence connects expectation, resurrection, and restoration without forcing these texts into one timetable.
literary_context: The references use apocalyptic vision in Daniel, a discourse in Matthew, pastoral reassurance in First Thessalonians, argument in First Corinthians, and a concluding vision in Revelation. Daniel uses symbolic figures and awakening imagery; Matthew uses cosmic signs and the Son of Man; Paul answers questions about deceased believers and resurrection; Revelation portrays the future as renewed creation. The genres shape how their images communicate hope, and they do not all answer the same question.
covenantal_significance: The passages ground future hope in God’s rule and promise of life. Daniel 7 depicts authority given to the human-like figure, and Daniel 12 speaks of awakening from death. Matthew 24 portrays gathering; First Thessalonians 4 offers comfort about the dead; First Corinthians 15 describes resurrection and the defeat of death; Revelation 21 envisions God dwelling with humanity in renewed creation. Together, these texts present hope as more than escape from the world, while leaving the details of timing and sequence unresolved in this record.
canonical_role: Eschatology serves as a theological anchor, connecting doctrinal concepts, canonical development, and related passages across Scripture.

related_objects.notes: Adds passage-level distinctions for bodily transformation, grief, unknown timing, and judgment.

interpretive_notes.note: Read Eschatology in its immediate context before generalizing.
Do not flatten distinct passages into one slogan; let the canon keep its own shape.
